stanzas: Üsküdar’a gider iken aldı da bir yağmur,
Kâtibimin setresi uzun eteği çamur.
Kâtip uykudan uyanmış gözleri mahmur.
Kâtip benim ben kâtibin el ne karışır,
Kâtibime kolalı da gömlek ne güzel yaraşır.
Üsküdar’a gider iken bir mendil buldum,
Mendilimin içine de lokum doldurdum.
Kâtibimi arar iken yanımda buldum.
Kâtip benim ben kâtibin el ne karışır,
Kâtibime kolalı da gömlek ne güzel yaraşır.
As [we] were going to Üsküdar, a rain came down on us,
my clerk's frock coat, its long skirt muddy.
The clerk has woken from sleep, his eyes heavy with sleep.
The clerk is mine, I am the clerk's, what business is it of strangers?
How well a starched shirt suits my clerk!
As I was going to Üsküdar, I found a handkerchief,
and into my handkerchief I filled Turkish delight.
As I was looking for my clerk, I found him at my side.
The clerk is mine, I am the clerk's, what business is it of strangers?
How well a starched shirt suits my clerk!

notes: line 1.1: 'gider iken aldı da bir yağmur' gives no subject for 'going'; 'we' is supplied from the sense (it can equally be 'I'); 'aldı' is literally 'took', i.e. the rain caught them. The particle 'da', put in to fill the tune (1.1, 2.2, 3.2), is not translated.
line 1.2: 'setre' is the long frock coat of Ottoman officials after the reforms of Mahmud II; 'uzun eteği çamur' is literally 'its long skirt mud'.
line 1.3: 'mahmur' is the languid, heavy look of eyes just woken (or drowsy, or after drink); 'heavy with sleep' is one reading.
Kâtip: a clerk or secretary (scribe). The singer's sex is not stated in the text; 'his' for the clerk follows the Turkish context (an Ottoman clerk), as Turkish has no gendered pronoun.
line 2.1: 'el' is 'other people, strangers'; 'el ne karışır' is 'why should others meddle'.
